paragraphs: Converting an image into markup involves recovering both symbols and their organization. When the markup represents a tree, a decoder that produces a flat string must express that hierarchy indirectly. The paper first uses toy problems to show that string decoders struggle with tree structures, with difficulties becoming more pronounced as structural complexity increases.

The proposed decoder generates the tree explicitly. At each sequential step, it produces a child node together with its parent node, forming a small subtree. These subtrees are then incorporated recurrently into the developing output. This makes parent-child relationships part of the generation process itself, rather than information that must be recovered from a serialized sequence.

Evaluations on mathematical and chemical formula recognition show substantial improvements over strong string decoder baselines. The findings support matching the decoder’s output structure to the structure of the markup: explicitly maintaining tree relationships helps the model handle the organization that makes these recognition tasks difficult.
icml-2020-a-tree-structured-decoder-for-.tldr: An explicit tree decoder improves mathematical and chemical formula recognition by generating parent-child relationships directly.

paragraphs: An architecture can guarantee that its transformations are invertible without being able to represent every continuous invertible transformation. This paper investigates that distinction for Neural ODEs and invertible residual networks, or i-ResNets. It shows that both architectures have restrictions on what they can approximate in their original form, despite their built-in invertibility.

The central result gives a way to overcome those restrictions by increasing the space in which the model operates. Any homeomorphism on a p-dimensional Euclidean space—a continuous invertible mapping whose inverse is also continuous—can be approximated by either architecture operating in 2p dimensions. Doubling the dimension is a sufficient construction established by the paper; the result does not assert that doubling is always necessary.

The paper also shows that adding a single linear output layer is sufficient to obtain universal approximation of continuous functions that need not be invertible. Together, these results clarify how extra dimensions and an output layer expand the expressive capabilities of otherwise constrained architectures.
icml-2020-approximation-capabilities-of-.tldr: Higher-dimensional constructions overcome approximation limits of Neural ODEs and i-ResNets, while a linear output layer enables approximation of non-invertible continuous functions.

paragraphs: Learning through trial and error becomes hazardous when failures can damage an agent or its surroundings. This paper studies a setting in which an agent first learns in source environments where failures are less consequential, then adapts to a target environment where mistakes carry substantial costs. The challenge is to keep learning despite unfamiliar dynamics while exploring cautiously.

The proposed approach, CARL, uses model-based reinforcement learning across varied source environments. It trains a probabilistic model that represents uncertainty about how actions change the environment and which states are catastrophic. During adaptation, the agent uses that prior experience to assess risk and plans to avoid actions that could lead to catastrophic states.

Experiments involving driving, cartpole balancing, and half-cheetah locomotion show that CARL develops cautious exploration behaviors. It obtains higher rewards with fewer failures than strong adaptation baselines in those experiments. These results support using learned uncertainty to guide relatively safer adaptation; the claim is improved risk management, rather than a guarantee that failures cannot occur.
icml-2020-cautious-adaptation-for-reinfo.tldr: CARL uses probabilistic models learned across source environments to adapt cautiously, achieving higher rewards with fewer failures in tested tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies games in which teammates share a utility function but act independently against an adversary. Its target is a Team-Maxmin Equilibrium, or TME. Computing this solution becomes difficult when the available strategies are so numerous that even representing the full strategy space exceeds memory limits.

Incremental Strategy Generation addresses large strategy spaces by avoiding enumeration of every pure strategy. The authors show that, in multiplayer games, this approach converges to a Nash equilibrium but may fail to reach a TME. They develop ISGT using the characterization of a TME as a Nash equilibrium that maximizes the team’s utility. They prove convergence to a TME and establish that the conditions used in ISGT cannot be relaxed.

A further variant, CISGT, starts ISGT from a strategy space obtained by computing an easier equilibrium close to a TME. This initialization improves scalability. Extensive experiments report speedups of orders of magnitude over both ISGT and the existing state-of-the-art TME algorithm on large games.
icml-2020-converging-to-team-maxmin-equi.tldr: The paper develops convergent incremental methods for team equilibria and an initialization strategy that greatly accelerates computation in large games.

paragraphs: A dynamic treatment regime specifies a sequence of treatment decisions based on a patient’s evolving treatment and covariate history. Learning such rules online can require extensive experimentation when the possible combinations of treatments and covariates are numerous. The paper describes a worst-case regret dependence on the size of this combined domain, explaining why ordinary exploration can become impractical.

The proposed improvement relies on having the causal diagram of the environment. By exploiting this structure, the authors show that regret can have an exponentially smaller dependence on the treatment-and-covariate domain. They develop two algorithms with corresponding bounds: OFU-DTR uses optimism under uncertainty, while PS-DTR uses posterior sampling to guide decisions.

The paper also introduces methods for accelerating these online procedures with abundant observational data, while recognizing that such data are biased. The contribution is a causal approach to reducing the burden of sequential experimentation. Its theoretical advantage is conditional on the supplied causal structure, rather than a claim that arbitrary treatment problems become easy to learn.
icml-2020-designing-optimal-dynamic-trea.tldr: Given a causal diagram, two reinforcement learning algorithms can substantially reduce regret when learning sequential treatment rules.

paragraphs: This paper considers federated classification in an unusually restricted setting: each user holds positive examples from only one class. During local updates, that user cannot access the features or model parameters for negative classes. Conventional distributed training can consequently produce poor or trivial classifiers because local learning lacks information that distinguishes one class from the others.

For classifiers based on embeddings, a particular failure is that all class representations may collapse to the same point. The proposed framework, Federated Averaging with Spreadout, or FedAwS, addresses this through a server-side geometric regularizer. After each federated round, the server encourages class embeddings to remain spread apart, adding separation that positive-only local updates do not provide.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that FedAwS can nearly match conventional learning in which users have negative labels available. They also extend the method to large output spaces. The result suggests that coordinating the geometry of class representations can compensate substantially for this restricted form of local supervision.
icml-2020-federated-learning-with-only-p.tldr: FedAwS separates class embeddings at the server so federated learning with only positive local labels can nearly match conventional training.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial imitation learning, or GAIL, learns a policy and a reward function from expert demonstrations. Neural networks have made this approach successful in practice, but empirical success leaves a theoretical question: can the learning procedure reach a globally optimal solution? This paper addresses that question through analysis of the optimization process.

The difficulty is that the policy and reward are learned through a minimax problem whose neural-network formulation is nonconvex and nonconcave. That structure makes global convergence difficult to establish. The authors analyze a gradient-based algorithm that alternates updates, tracking how the coupled optimization progresses toward its solution.

Their result establishes sublinear convergence to a global optimum for the algorithm they study. It therefore provides both a destination guarantee and a characterization of convergence speed, rather than merely evidence that training performs well in examples. The contribution connects neural GAIL’s practical use with formal optimization theory; it concerns the analyzed procedure, not a blanket guarantee for every neural imitation-learning implementation.
icml-2020-generative-adversarial-imitati.tldr: The paper proves sublinear convergence to a global optimum for an alternating gradient algorithm for neural-network GAIL.

paragraphs: Graph convolution can support recommendation by processing relationships in graph data, but its computational cost becomes substantial on large graphs. The paper argues that the simplifications used in existing graph convolutional networks sacrifice too much of the original operation’s effectiveness. It seeks a way to retain that operation while making its use practical at larger scales.

The proposed Low-pass Collaborative Filter, or LCF, has two connected purposes. It removes noise attributed to exposure and quantization in observed data, and it reduces the computational complexity of graph convolution. The method is presented as preserving the convolution’s effectiveness while reducing its cost, addressing the tradeoff that motivates the work.

Experiments report improvements in both the effectiveness and efficiency of graph convolution, with the resulting network significantly outperforming existing GCNs in the evaluated setting. The contribution is therefore a filtering approach that tackles noisy recommendation observations and expensive graph computation together. Its stated findings concern these experimental comparisons, rather than a universal ranking of all recommendation methods.
icml-2020-graph-convolutional-network-fo.tldr: A low-pass collaborative filter reduces noise and computation in graph convolution, improving recommendation effectiveness and efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Graph Random Neural Features, or GRNF, converts graphs into real-valued vectors using a family of graph neural networks. The aim is to make graph data usable by vector-based methods while retaining meaningful structural differences. The representation also handles graph isomorphism, so alternative descriptions of the same graph structure are treated appropriately.

The method preserves the metric structure of the graph domain in probability. It supplies explicit embeddings and supports efficient approximation of graph distances and complete kernel functions. The authors also provide a criterion for choosing the embedding dimension, making the tradeoff between approximation accuracy and computational cost an explicit part of using the method.

GRNF can serve as input to traditional processing methods or as a training-free input layer for a graph neural network. Its theory establishes that the underlying graph distance is a metric and can distinguish every pair of non-isomorphic graphs. That exact property of the distance should be distinguished from the probabilistic preservation offered by the vector approximation.
icml-2020-graph-random-neural-features-f.tldr: GRNF maps graphs to vectors that preserve graph distances in probability, with an explicit accuracy–computation tradeoff.

paragraphs: Neural networks can be viewed as graphs, but that viewpoint alone does not explain how their connection patterns affect prediction. This paper introduces a relational graph representation to investigate that relationship systematically. In this representation, a layer of network computation corresponds to a round of messages exchanged along the graph’s connections.

Using this formulation, the authors identify a region of graph structures associated with significantly better predictive performance. They report that performance varies approximately smoothly with two graph properties: the clustering coefficient, which describes local connectedness, and average path length, which describes how far apart nodes are through graph connections. This connects architecture quality to measurable structural characteristics.

The findings are consistent across many tasks and datasets, and the favorable region can be identified efficiently. The authors also observe that top-performing networks have graph structures similar to real biological neural networks. Together, these observations suggest a route to architectural design based on connectivity patterns, while the biological similarity remains an observed structural relationship.
icml-2020-graph-structure-of-neural-netw.tldr: A relational graph representation reveals connectivity patterns associated with stronger neural-network prediction across multiple tasks and datasets.

paragraphs: Structured bandit problems involve repeated decisions whose actions and observations have dependencies that a simple list of unrelated choices cannot capture. This paper introduces influence diagram bandits, using graphical models to represent relationships among actions, hidden variables, and observations. The framework brings together and extends models including combinatorial semi-bandits, cascading bandits, and low-rank bandits.

The learning algorithms maintain a structured posterior distribution over the model’s unknown parameters, either exactly or approximately. To choose an action, they sample parameters from that posterior and exploit the influence diagram’s structure to find the most optimistic action for the sampled model. Thus, both uncertainty and dependencies enter the decision process.

Experiments cover three structured bandit problems. The proposed algorithms perform as well as or better than state-of-the-art methods tailored to those individual problems. This supports the value of a shared modeling and learning framework: preserving problem structure can allow a general approach to compete with specialized algorithms, while also accommodating a broader family of decision problems.
icml-2020-graphical-models-meet-bandits-.tldr: Influence diagram bandits combine graphical models with posterior sampling to handle structured decisions and compete with specialized methods.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations in high-dimensional environments presents a challenge beyond reproducing observed behavior: an agent must explore effectively if it is to surpass its demonstrator. The paper focuses on this problem in settings such as Atari, where it reports that most inverse reinforcement learning methods struggle to exceed demonstration performance.

The proposed reward-learning module uses a generative model to produce intrinsic reward signals. It improves forward state-transition modeling and backward action encoding, strengthening its model of the environment’s dynamics. The authors connect these capabilities to two benefits: conveying the demonstrator’s underlying intention and supporting better exploration by the imitation agent.

On multiple Atari games, the method outperforms state-of-the-art inverse reinforcement learning approaches, including when supplied with a one-life demonstration. Its strongest reported result reaches up to five times the demonstration’s performance. That figure describes the reported upper end of the empirical results, while the broader finding is that dynamics-informed intrinsic rewards can help imitation move beyond the behavior directly demonstrated.
icml-2020-intrinsic-reward-driven-imitat.tldr: A generative reward module improves imitation and exploration on Atari, with reported performance reaching up to five times the demonstration.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation adjusts a classifier when its training and test data follow different distributions. Methods that learn domain-invariant representations commonly assume the source labels are correct. This paper investigates what happens when that assumption fails, examining how noisy source labels can harm adaptation methods across different scenarios.

The proposed denoising Conditional Invariant Component framework, or DCIC, focuses on generalized target shift. In this setting, both class frequencies and the distribution of inputs within each class may change between domains. The framework uses noisy labeled source examples together with unlabeled target examples, addressing label corruption and distribution change within the same adaptation problem.

The authors establish theoretical guarantees for extracting invariant representations and estimating target-domain class frequencies without bias in the setting they analyze. They also prove the existence of a method that can substantially reduce the adverse effect of noisy source labels. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support DCIC’s effectiveness, connecting the theoretical treatment of label noise to observed adaptation improvements.
icml-2020-label-noise-robust-domain-adap.tldr: DCIC addresses noisy source labels under generalized target shift, with guarantees for invariant representations and unbiased target class-frequency estimation.

paragraphs: Generating long sequences of behavior with adjustable styles requires more than producing varied actions. A policy must express several requested style properties at once, and the number of possible combinations can grow rapidly. This paper addresses both how those properties should be specified and how learning can encourage generated behavior to satisfy them.

The framework uses programmatic labeling functions to define the styles that users can control. It then formalizes style-consistency as a learning objective: the requested styles and the styles exhibited by generated behavior should agree. Because this requirement becomes part of the objective, conventional policy-learning approaches can be used to learn the controllable policies.

The authors evaluate the framework using demonstrations from professional basketball players and agents in the MuJoCo physics environment. They report that approaches without explicit style-consistency fail to generate diverse behaviors, while their policies can be calibrated to as many as 1,024 style combinations. The findings support directly training for simultaneous style adherence when controlling long-term behavior.
icml-2020-learning-calibratable-policies.tldr: Programmatic style definitions and an explicit consistency objective enable policies calibrated to up to 1,024 combinations of behavioral styles.

paragraphs: This paper studies exploration in episodic reinforcement learning with approximately linear action-value functions. Its central condition is low inherent Bellman error, which measures how far Bellman updates move outside the chosen function class. The authors show that this condition is strictly more general than the low-rank or linear MDP assumption used in earlier work.

They provide an algorithm with a high-probability regret bound containing a learning term proportional to the square root of the number of episodes and an approximation-error term proportional to the number of episodes. The latter amplifies inherent Bellman error only by the square root of the feature dimension at each timestep. A matching lower bound establishes optimality up to constants and logarithmic factors.

These results show that statistically efficient exploration is possible under assumptions normally used for batch value approximation. For a one-step horizon, the method becomes LinUCB with an exploration parameter adapted to misspecification. Computational tractability remains open for the MDP setting, so the established efficiency is statistical rather than a complete computational guarantee.
icml-2020-learning-near-optimal-policies.tldr: Low inherent Bellman error permits statistically optimal exploration under broader assumptions than linear MDPs, though computational tractability remains open.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer a buyer’s valuations by observing purchases under different prices. The buyer is a k-demand agent: values add across goods when receiving at most k items, but the buyer has no interest in additional items beyond that limit. This restriction gives the learning problem a specific structure.

In the active-learning version, the learner chooses the prices and observes the resulting purchases. The authors introduce a biased binary search algorithm that generalizes ordinary binary search to this preference-elicitation problem. They establish upper bounds on the number of queries and complementary lower bounds that match up to lower-order terms, settling the query complexity at that precision.

The passive version removes control over prices, which instead come from a distribution. In the probably approximately correct learning model, the authors show that any empirical risk minimizer has sample complexity within a factor of approximately k, allowing logarithmic factors, of optimal. The results distinguish what can be learned through deliberate price experiments from what can be learned through observation.
icml-2020-learning-the-valuations-of-a-k.tldr: The paper establishes near-matching learning bounds for inferring a k-demand buyer’s valuations from actively chosen or passively observed prices.

paragraphs: Multi-objective black-box optimization seeks useful tradeoffs among competing objectives using only evaluations at selected inputs. Its target is the Pareto frontier, rather than a single best scalar value. This paper measures progress through the hypervolume indicator, which assesses the dominated volume covered by the full collection of selected solutions.

The authors introduce a hypervolume scalarization that converts multiple objectives into a scalar quantity. Drawing these scalarizations from an appropriately chosen distribution allows efficient approximation of the hypervolume indicator. This relationship gives a principled connection between optimizing individual scalar objectives and improving coverage of the multi-objective solution set.

For Bayesian optimization using Thompson Sampling or Upper Confidence Bound, the paper proves convergence to the whole Pareto frontier through tight hypervolume regret bounds of square-root order in the number of evaluations, up to logarithmic factors. It also shows how any single-objective optimization procedure with proven convergence can be converted into a multi-objective procedure with convergence guarantees, broadening the framework beyond those particular acquisition rules.
icml-2020-random-hypervolume-scalarizati.tldr: Random hypervolume scalarizations turn convergent single-objective optimization into multi-objective optimization with provable Pareto-frontier convergence.

paragraphs: Meta-transfer learning combines learning across tasks with transferring prior knowledge as tasks change over time. This paper examines Sequential Neural Processes, or SNP, in that setting and empirically finds underfitting in the functions they infer. It also finds that standard attention mechanisms do not provide the same effective remedy seen in the meta-learning setting.

The authors propose Recurrent Memory Reconstruction, or RMR, to make attention useful when tasks are dynamic and available context can be small. RMR supplies an imaginary context that is recurrently updated and reconstructed through interaction. The key change is therefore the context available to attention, with an evolving memory supporting the learning process.

Combining RMR with SNP produces Attentive Sequential Neural Processes-RMR. Across various tasks, this model significantly outperforms the evaluated baselines. The experiments support the importance of recurrently reconstructed context for effective attention in the studied meta-transfer setting, while showing why simply adding a standard attention mechanism did not resolve the observed underfitting problem.
icml-2020-robustifying-sequential-neural.tldr: Recurrently reconstructed imaginary context makes attention effective for Sequential Neural Processes and improves performance across tested changing-task settings.

paragraphs: Text models can be sensitive to input changes that should leave the intended meaning intact. This paper addresses robustness to task-relevant edits through a language for specifying string transformations programmatically. Users can describe changes such as insertions, deletions, substitutions, and swaps, making the desired robustness target explicit.

The training approach combines search-based adversarial techniques with abstraction-based techniques. It decomposes a user-defined transformation specification into two components, choosing one suited to search and another suited to abstraction. This allows the method to use the advantages of both approaches within a single adversarial-training procedure rather than treating all specified transformations identically.

The authors train models on AG and SST2 and show robustness to combinations of transformations that imitate spelling mistakes and other meaning-preserving changes. The contribution is both a flexible way to express relevant perturbations and a method for training against them. The reported robustness concerns the user-defined combinations studied, with the specification determining which kinds of input changes the training addresses.
icml-2020-robustness-to-programmable-str.tldr: A programmable transformation language and combined search-and-abstraction training improve text-model robustness to specified combinations of string edits.

paragraphs: Weighted model integration, or WMI, supports probabilistic reasoning with both discrete and continuous variables under logical and arithmetic constraints. Its expressive language can capture complex dependencies, but exploiting those dependencies computationally is difficult. The paper argues that existing solvers either ignore the dependency structure or support structures that are too restrictive.

The authors derive a factorized form of WMI computation and use it to build MP-WMI, a message-passing solver. This formulation enables exact inference across the full class of tree-structured WMI problems. The structural scope matters: the stated exact-inference capability applies to tree-structured problems, rather than all possible dependency graphs.

MP-WMI also shares computation across different queries, a capability called inter-query amortization. For example, it can compute all marginal densities simultaneously instead of treating each as an independent task. Experiments show dramatic improvements over existing WMI solvers across a large benchmark collection. The contribution combines broader structural support with reusable computation to make expressive hybrid probabilistic inference more scalable.
icml-2020-scaling-up-hybrid-probabilisti.tldr: MP-WMI uses factorization and message passing for exact tree-structured hybrid inference while sharing computation across queries.

paragraphs: Bootstrap methods assess statistical uncertainty, but applying them to massive data spread across many machines creates computational and communication burdens. This paper proposes a distributed bootstrap procedure designed to retain statistical efficiency while reducing that work. Its central choice is to carry out the bootstrap on a coordinating master machine using information received from workers.

The workers supply gradients, and the master applies a multiplier bootstrap to those gradients. The procedure does not require fitting the model repeatedly. It also avoids the over-resampling that the abstract identifies as typical of existing approaches. These choices concentrate the uncertainty calculation at the master rather than repeatedly distributing model-fitting work across the data.

The authors prove optimal statistical efficiency with minimal communication for their method, and simulations support the theoretical results. The significance is that reducing computation and data exchange need not sacrifice the statistical efficiency established by the analysis. The method specifically achieves this through gradient-based bootstrap computation, connecting distributed learning information with uncertainty estimation.
icml-2020-simultaneous-inference-for-mas.tldr: A master-side multiplier bootstrap uses worker gradients to achieve optimal statistical efficiency without repeated model fitting or over-resampling.

paragraphs: A divergence is intended to compare probability distributions, but the comparison may not exist when the distributions have different supports or lack defined densities. This paper addresses that obstacle by defining Spread Divergence on modified versions of the two distributions. The starting point is therefore to make a meaningful comparison possible through an explicit transformation.

The authors describe sufficient conditions under which the resulting divergence exists. They also parameterize the spread and learn it to maximize the discriminatory power of a chosen divergence. This gives the modification an active role: it is used both to support a well-defined comparison and to improve how effectively that comparison distinguishes distributions.

The paper presents examples of training implicit generative models with Spread Divergence, covering linear Independent Components Analysis models and nonlinear Deep Generative Networks. These examples connect the mathematical construction to model training. The existence result remains a sufficient-condition statement, while the learnable spread offers a way to adapt the comparison rather than relying on one fixed modification.
icml-2020-spread-divergence-036120d051.tldr: Spread Divergence compares modified distributions under sufficient existence conditions and learns the modification to strengthen discrimination.

paragraphs: Deep energy-based models offer flexible ways to represent probability distributions, but training is difficult because their partition function is intractable. Standard training typically uses maximum likelihood, with contrastive divergence approximating the gradient associated with KL divergence. This paper asks how to train these models using other members of the broader f-divergence family.

The proposed f-EBM framework uses a variational formulation that supports any desired f-divergence. The authors introduce a corresponding optimization algorithm and analyze it using nonlinear dynamical systems theory. They prove a local convergence property, establishing behavior near a solution rather than a global convergence guarantee from arbitrary starting points.

Experiments show that f-EBM outperforms contrastive divergence and that choosing divergences other than KL can benefit energy-based model training. The contribution separates the model’s flexible distribution representation from a fixed choice of training divergence. It provides both an optimization framework for making that choice and empirical evidence that the choice can affect the quality of training.
icml-2020-training-deep-energy-based-mod.tldr: f-EBM trains energy-based models with any chosen f-divergence, with a local convergence result and empirical gains over contrastive divergence.

paragraphs: Self-supervision has been useful for learning image representations, but its benefits for graph convolutional networks require separate investigation. This paper systematically studies how to incorporate self-supervision into GCNs and when doing so improves their behavior. It treats the design of the auxiliary task and the way it enters training as linked decisions.

The authors examine three incorporation mechanisms, discussing limitations of pretraining followed by finetuning and of self-training before focusing on multi-task learning. They propose three self-supervised tasks for GCNs, supported by theoretical rationales and numerical comparisons. They also integrate multi-task self-supervision into graph adversarial training to investigate robustness.

The results show gains in generalizability and robustness when the task forms and incorporation mechanisms are appropriately designed. That qualification is central to the finding: the paper supports particular ways of introducing self-supervision, rather than claiming that any auxiliary task will help. Its contribution is an organized assessment of the choices that determine whether self-supervision improves graph learning.
icml-2020-when-does-self-supervision-hel.tldr: Self-supervision improves GCN generalizability and robustness when its auxiliary tasks and training mechanisms are appropriately designed.

paragraphs: Incremental few-shot learning asks a model to recognize new categories from very few labeled examples while retaining knowledge of existing categories. XtarNet addresses this by adapting the representation used for classification to the new task. It starts with a backbone network pretrained on base categories and adds modules meta-trained across learning episodes.

For a new task, the additional modules produce a novel feature that is mixed with the base feature from the pretrained backbone. Meta-trained modules also control that combination. The resulting task-adaptive representation contains information useful for recognizing both base and novel categories, allowing both classifiers to adapt quickly to the task.

Experiments on standard image datasets report state-of-the-art incremental few-shot performance. The authors also apply the representation idea alongside existing incremental few-shot methods, with extensive simulations showing significant improvements. These findings make the contribution broader than one classifier design: learning how to combine established features with task-specific information can also strengthen other methods facing the same old-and-new category challenge.
icml-2020-xtarnet-learning-to-extract-ta.tldr: XtarNet learns to mix pretrained and task-specific features so classifiers can recognize new categories from few examples while retaining base-category knowledge.
